# Openings, Hooks and First Pages

Category `open` of the Writing Creativity Database.

The highest-leverage file in the set per word written. Readers, commissioners and audiences decide early: a screenplay gets about ten pages, a novel about two, a reel about one second. Nothing else in this database is judged on so little material.

**Part 1 of 3.** 28 cards across the opening promise, first-page hooks, screen openings, short-form openings, and the failure modes.

## The opening promise

### The Contract Opening

**Also called:** the promise of the premise, the tonal handshake
**What it is:** The opening states what kind of experience this will be — its tone, its pace, its rules, its moral temperature — so that everything after it is either kept or deliberately broken.
**Effect on the audience:** Trust. An audience that knows what it has been promised relaxes into the work; one that does not spends the first act deciding what it is watching instead of watching it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every form, and especially any work with an unusual register — a comedy about a funeral, a documentary with reconstruction, a heritage piece that will use humour. The rule: whatever is in the first three minutes, the audience will expect for the whole running time, so do not open on a tone you cannot sustain. A prologue of violence on a film that contains no other violence is a broken contract, and audiences punish that harder than they punish a slow start.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: all
**Avoid when:** The deliberate mismatch is the point, as in a horror that opens as a romantic comedy. That works, but it is a different technique and it must pay the mismatch off explicitly, not merely abandon it.
**Example:**
> A wedding. The camera stays on the one guest not clapping.
> The promise: this is a story about a family, told from the outside.

`open.contract_opening`

### Opening Image, Answered

**Also called:** the bookend open, the first frame
**What it is:** The opening states the starting condition in a single concrete image or moment, chosen so that a mirrored final image can measure the whole distance travelled.
**Effect on the audience:** They feel the arc without anyone describing it. Change is only legible against a fixed reference, and this is the reference.
**Used for and where it works best:** Features, animation, novels, anything with a genuine arc. It must be a *condition*, not atmosphere — a man eating alone at a table for six is an opening image; a moody street is not. Design it backwards: decide the final image first, then build its opposite.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Animation Feature, Novel, Limited Series, Short Film, Documentary | genres: Drama, Coming of Age, Family Drama, Romance, Heritage, Tragedy, Comedy
**Avoid when:** Episodic work that resets, where there is no distance to measure. Also avoid when the mirror at the end would be too neat — a final image that merely inverts the first can feel like a trick rather than a conclusion. One element changed is stronger than a full reversal.
**Example:**
> **Open:** he sets six places at the table and eats alone.
> **Close:** he sets six places at the table, and this time he does not eat alone.

**Yields to:** `open.episode_opening` — Episodic work that resets, no distance to measure.  
`open.opening_image_answered`

### The Question Planted First

**Also called:** the opening enigma, the deferred explanation
**What it is:** The opening presents something the audience cannot yet explain — an object, a behaviour, a line, a discrepancy — and does not explain it.
**Effect on the audience:** Forward pull that costs nothing. A question is cheaper than a mystery and works in any genre.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any opening that must hold attention before the audience cares about anyone. It is the correct solution when the story's first act is necessarily slow: the unexplained thing carries the reader until the characters can. The question must be *specific* — not "something is wrong" but "why is she carrying two phones".
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Feature Film, One-Hour Drama, Podcast, Limited Series, Short Film | genres: Mystery, Thriller, Drama, Literary, Crime, Psychological, Noir
**Avoid when:** The answer is trivial. An audience that waits ninety minutes for a small answer feels cheated, and the technique's whole credit is spent. Also avoid stacking more than two open questions in an opening, which produces confusion rather than intrigue.
**Example:**
> First line: *Last winter I gave my brother's coat to a man I had never met, and I would do it again.*

**Yields to:** `open.mystery_discovery` — Fair-play mystery needing a verifiable fact.  
`open.question_planted_first`

### Theme Stated Early

**Also called:** the thematic line, the argument spoken
**What it is:** Someone states the story's argument out loud, near the beginning, usually to a protagonist not ready to hear it and usually in a scene about something else.
**Effect on the audience:** They are handed the measuring stick before the measuring starts, which is what lets an ending feel inevitable rather than arbitrary.
**Used for and where it works best:** Features and animation, where the beat has a known page. The two rules that make it invisible: it must be said by someone other than the protagonist, and the protagonist must disagree or ignore it. Delivered as agreement, it becomes a summary of the film.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Animation Feature, Novel, Limited Series | genres: Drama, Comedy, Family, Coming of Age, Romance, Sports, Redemption
**Avoid when:** The work has no argument to state — pure adventure, most procedural, much comedy. Forcing one produces a line the audience recognises as the moral before the story has earned it.
**Example:**
> "You'd give the shirt off your back, and that's exactly the problem."
> "It's a shirt."

**Yields to:** `open.comedy_premise_statement` — Comedy or situation work with no argument to state.  
`open.theme_stated_early`

## First-page hooks

### The Character Hook

**Also called:** the person-first open, hooking on voice
**What it is:** The opening leads with a specific, particular person rather than with a situation — their voice, their attention, their particular way of being wrong about something.
**Effect on the audience:** Attachment before plot. Readers are hooked by character more often than by event; a distinctive person doing nothing much holds better than a generic person in danger.
**Used for and where it works best:** First-person prose, memoir, character-led drama and comedy, and any work whose plot takes a while to start. This is also the correct hook when the story genuinely has no early incident — instead of inventing a false one, lead with a person worth following. The rule: particularity, not likeability. A specific unpleasant person outperforms a vague pleasant one.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Memoir, Short Story, One-Hour Drama, Half-Hour Comedy, Podcast, Stage Play | genres: Literary, Comedy, Drama, Coming of Age, Social Drama, Family Drama
**Avoid when:** Plot-forward genre work where the reader came for the machine, and short-form, which has no time to develop a voice before the scroll.
**Example:**
> *I have never in my life returned a library book on time, and I want to be clear that this is a decision.*

**Yields to:** `open.situation_hook` — Plot-forward genre work, reader came for the machine.  
`open.character_hook`

### The Situation Hook

**Also called:** in medias res, dropping into trouble
**What it is:** The opening begins inside an event already in progress, with the explanation withheld until the reader is committed.
**Effect on the audience:** Immediate momentum plus a mild puzzle, because they are reconstructing the situation while it unfolds.
**Used for and where it works best:** Thrillers, action, most commercial fiction, and any project that must survive a first-ten-pages read. The craft rule that separates it from confusion: the reader must be able to answer *who wants what, right now* within a paragraph, even if they cannot answer *why* for fifty pages.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Novel, One-Hour Drama, Short Film, Vertical Micro-Drama, Game Narrative | genres: Thriller, Crime, Action, Adventure, Science Fiction, Horror, Mystery
**Avoid when:** It is being used to hide a slow story. An in-medias-res opening followed by forty pages of backstory is the most common bait-and-switch in unsold manuscripts, and readers recognise it instantly.
**Example:**
> *The third time the alarm went off, Hana stopped pretending it was a drill and took the stairs.*

**Yields to:** `open.question_planted_first` — First act is genuinely slow, not fast.  
`open.situation_hook`

### The Voice Hook

**Also called:** the announced narrator, style as promise
**What it is:** The opening's distinction is entirely in how it is written rather than in what happens — rhythm, register, an unusual angle of attention.
**Effect on the audience:** Confidence in the writer. A reader who trusts the prose will grant an enormous amount of patience on plot.
**Used for and where it works best:** Literary fiction, essay, memoir, narrative podcast, and any first-person work. It is the only hook that works with genuinely no incident at all. It is also the riskiest, because a voice that cannot sustain itself for a chapter is worse than no voice.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Memoir, Essay, Short Story, Podcast, Audio Drama | genres: Literary, Comedy, Satire, Social Drama, Heritage, Historical
**Avoid when:** Screenwriting, where the reader is assessing a film and not your prose, and the industry convention reads stylised action lines as amateur. Also avoid in translation-bound work, where voice is the first thing lost.
**Example:**
> *My father built three houses and lived in none of them, which tells you most of what you need to know about my father and almost nothing about the houses.*

**Yields to:** `open.subtitled_open` — Translation-bound work, where voice is lost first.  
`open.voice_hook`

### The Rule of the World

**Also called:** the world premise stated, the first law
**What it is:** The opening establishes one concrete rule that governs this world — social, physical, economic or legal — and demonstrates it working rather than explaining it.
**Effect on the audience:** Orientation without exposition. A single demonstrated rule implies a whole system, and the audience builds the rest themselves.
**Used for and where it works best:** Science fiction, fantasy, historical, heritage, and any workplace or closed community. Demonstrate the rule on a minor character first, then apply it to the protagonist — that sequence teaches the rule and raises the stakes in two beats. It is also the cleanest opening for heritage work, where the audience needs the period's logic before its events.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Novel, Limited Series, Animation Feature, Game Narrative, Heritage Documentary | genres: Science Fiction, Fantasy, Historical, Heritage, Dystopia, Western, Social Drama
**Avoid when:** The world is the audience's own. Establishing a rule everyone already lives under wastes the opening and reads as condescension.
**Example:**
> The queue moves when the man at the window stands up. He has been sitting for two hours. Nobody has spoken to him. When he stands, forty people step forward one pace.

**Yields to:** `open.ordinary_day_slightly_wrong` — The world is the audience's own.  
`open.rule_of_the_world`

### The Object Opening

**Also called:** opening on a thing, the loaded detail
**What it is:** The opening rests on a single physical object, examined closely, which will matter later.
**Effect on the audience:** A held breath. An object given weight before it has meaning creates anticipation with no information.
**Used for and where it works best:** Crime, literary fiction, heritage and documentary. It is the most economical way to open a story whose subject is the past, because an object carries time without a flashback. Pair it with a payoff card — the object must return, or the opening was decoration.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Novel, Short Film, Documentary, Heritage Documentary, Short Story | genres: Crime, Literary, Heritage, Historical, Drama, Mystery, War
**Avoid when:** The object is symbolic rather than functional. An object that exists only to mean something announces the writer; the strongest version is an ordinary object that acquires meaning through use.
**Example:**
> A house key on a ring with no other keys on it. The tag says a street name in a city eight hundred kilometres away.

`open.object_opening`

### The Ordinary Day, Slightly Wrong

**Also called:** the disturbed routine, one degree off
**What it is:** The opening presents a normal routine in which exactly one element is not right, and nobody in the scene remarks on it.
**Effect on the audience:** Unease they cannot immediately justify, which is the most durable opening state because it does not spend anything.
**Used for and where it works best:** Horror, psychological drama, literary fiction, and any story about a situation the characters have normalised. The single wrong element must be small enough that the characters' silence is plausible. Two wrong elements is a different genre.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Novel, One-Hour Drama, Short Film, Limited Series | genres: Horror, Psychological, Literary, Social Drama, Science Fiction, Drama, Mystery
**Avoid when:** The story is not going to justify the wrongness. This opening writes a cheque the third act must cash.
**Example:**
> Breakfast, three people, the radio on. There are four cups on the table and nobody moves the fourth.

**Yields to:** `open.last_ordinary_day` — The wrongness will never be justified.  
`open.ordinary_day_slightly_wrong`

## Screen openings

### The Cold Open

**Also called:** the teaser, the pre-titles sequence
**What it is:** A self-contained scene before the title sequence, designed to seize attention. In drama it sets tone or raises stakes; in comedy it works as an elaborate opening joke; in either case it is often not tied to the episode's main plot.
**Effect on the audience:** A reason to stay through the titles, which is the specific moment a broadcast or streaming audience leaves.
**Used for and where it works best:** Television of every length, and increasingly features. The strongest cold opens are complete in themselves — they have their own small turn — so that the audience feels they have already been given something. In procedural it is conventionally the crime; in comedy it is conventionally unrelated, and that unrelatedness is the pleasure.
**Best in:** formats: One-Hour Drama, Half-Hour Comedy, Limited Series, Web Series, Feature Film, Podcast | genres: Crime, Procedural, Comedy, Thriller, Drama, Science Fiction, Horror
**Avoid when:** It exists only to show something exciting that the show cannot sustain. Also avoid when the cold open is stronger than everything after it, which is a structural warning rather than a success.
**Example:**
> Two minutes: a man teaches his daughter to reverse a car. She scrapes a wall. He laughs.
> Titles.
> He is not in the rest of the episode. He is the reason for it.

`open.cold_open`

### The Title-Delayed Open

**Also called:** the long pre-title, holding the card
**What it is:** The title is withheld until an unusually late point — ten minutes, twenty, occasionally the end — so that it lands on a moment rather than on a start.
**Effect on the audience:** A hard punctuation mark placed where the writer wants it. The title arriving after a reversal reframes everything before it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Features and limited series with a strong first turn. Place the card immediately after the moment that defines the film's real subject, so the title becomes a comment on that moment. It also solves a specific problem: a film whose true premise only becomes clear after the first act.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Limited Series, Short Film, Documentary | genres: Thriller, Drama, Crime, Horror, Science Fiction, Literary, War
**Avoid when:** The pre-title material is not strong enough to hold without the promise of a beginning. Also avoid in television with fixed act structures and in any format with an advertising break convention.
**Example:**
> Twelve minutes in, she opens the envelope and reads the name.
> Cut to black. **TITLE.**

**Yields to:** `open.cold_open` — Television with fixed act structure or ad breaks.  
`open.title_delayed`

### Enter on the Answer

**Also called:** the pre-lapped opening, arriving mid-reply
**What it is:** The work opens on the answer to a question the audience never heard, and they reconstruct the question from the reply.
**Effect on the audience:** Engagement inside two seconds, plus a small puzzle, at no cost in runtime.
**Used for and where it works best:** Short-form above all — reels, vertical micro-drama, episode openings — where the first second decides retention. It is also excellent for a feature that must start fast without an action beat. The reconstructed question must be inferable within about a line, or the audience is lost rather than intrigued.
**Best in:** formats: Vertical Micro-Drama, Reels/Shorts, One-Hour Drama, Feature Film, Podcast, Half-Hour Comedy | genres: Thriller, Crime, Comedy, Melodrama, Drama, Romance
**Avoid when:** Used more than twice in a work, where it becomes a tic. Also avoid when the withheld question carries plot-critical information.
**Example:**
> **First line:** "Because she asked me not to, that's why."

**Yields to:** `open.open_mid_situation` — The withheld question carries plot-critical information.  
`open.enter_on_the_answer`

### The Scale Reveal Opening

**Also called:** the pull-back open, the widening first shot
**What it is:** The opening begins on a detail and widens — or begins wide and closes — so that the first information the audience receives is deliberately partial and is then corrected.
**Effect on the audience:** A small controlled shock, and an immediate lesson that this story will withhold context.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any work that needs scale established: war, epic, disaster, heritage, science fiction. In prose the equivalent is opening on a sensory detail and widening in the second paragraph. It is also an efficient way to make a low-budget or generated production feel large, since the reveal does the work rather than the asset.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Animation Feature, Documentary, Heritage Documentary, Novel, Short Film, Game Narrative | genres: War, Heritage, Historical, Science Fiction, Epic, Disaster, Survival
**Avoid when:** The correction is not meaningful. A widening that reveals nothing the audience cares about is a camera move, not an opening.
**Example:**
> A hand smoothing cloth. The cloth is a flag. The flag covers a body. The bodies continue past the edge of the frame.

**Yields to:** `open.object_opening` — The widening corrects nothing worth correcting.  
`open.scale_reveal`

### The Voiceover Open

**Also called:** the narrated opening, the framed beginning
**What it is:** A narrating voice opens the work, establishing a perspective, a time position, or a knowledge gap between narrator and events.
**Effect on the audience:** Instant orientation and instant tone — the two things an opening most needs and most struggles to deliver simultaneously.
**Used for and where it works best:** Documentary, memoir adaptation, heritage, crime, and any story told from a later vantage point. The rule that keeps it from being lazy: the narration must know something the scene does not, or be wrong about something the scene shows. A voice that describes what is visible is redundancy with music under it.
**Best in:** formats: Documentary, Heritage Documentary, Feature Film, Novel, Podcast, Animation Feature | genres: Crime, Heritage, Historical, Literary, Noir, Comedy, War
**Avoid when:** It is being used to deliver exposition the scenes should carry. This is the most frequently added and most frequently removed element in post-production, which is itself the diagnosis.
**Example:**
> *My uncle owned the only telephone on the street, which made him the most important man in it and the least trusted.*

**Yields to:** `open.rule_of_the_world` — Narration is carrying exposition a scene should demonstrate.  
`open.voiceover_open`

## Short-form openings

### The First-Second Hook

**Also called:** the scroll-stopper, the thumb-stop
**What it is:** A deliberate device placed in the first one to three seconds whose only job is to prevent a scroll: a blunt claim, an unexpected image, a sound arriving before its source is understood, a pattern interrupt.
**Effect on the audience:** Retention, measured. In short-form the first one to three seconds decide the outcome of the whole piece more than anything that follows.
**Used for and where it works best:** Reels, Shorts, TikTok, vertical micro-drama, and any paid social. The working hook types are pattern interrupt, the blunt claim, the mistake list, the process breakdown, and the demonstration. The promise being made is one of four: a **result**, a **reveal**, a **lesson**, or **tension** — decide which before writing anything else.
**Best in:** formats: Reels/Shorts, Vertical Micro-Drama, Advertising, Explainer, Web Series | genres: Comedy, Melodrama, Educational, Advocacy, Thriller, Lifestyle
**Avoid when:** Long-form, where a first-second device reads as desperation. And never make a hook the piece does not pay: a promised result that never arrives costs more than a weak opening, because it trains the audience to distrust the account.
**Shelf life:** dated — review 2027-09. Platform ranking signals and the exact retention window are current 2026 practice. The underlying craft — make a specific promise in the first moment and pay it — is durable.
**Example:**
> *"I was wrong about this for eleven years."*

**Yields to:** `open.stated_promise` — Long-form, where a one-second device reads as desperation.  
`open.first_second_hook`

### Open Mid-Situation

**Also called:** no arrival, the started scene
**What it is:** In short-form, there is no establishing, no arrival, no greeting. The piece begins at the point of maximum existing pressure.
**Effect on the audience:** They are already inside before they have decided to be.
**Used for and where it works best:** Vertical micro-drama and serialised reels, where it is not a choice but a condition of the format — episode length is dictated by attention and cliffhanger rhythm, not by story content, so there is no runtime for arrival at all. Pair with `dial.exposition_accusation`, which is how the missing context gets delivered later. In prose flash, whose reader controls the pace, the same start is a choice made for compression rather than a condition of the format: `struct.flash_fiction` applies it to the whole piece.
**Best in:** formats: Vertical Micro-Drama, Reels/Shorts, Web Series, Advertising | genres: Melodrama, Revenge, Romance, Family Drama, Crime, Thriller
**Avoid when:** The audience needs to know where they are to feel anything. Some short-form still requires a location beat; the test is whether the emotional content survives without it.
**Example:**
> The episode's first frame: she is already holding the test result, and he is already in the doorway.

**Yields to:** `open.orientation_vs_intrigue` — Audience needs spatial footing to feel anything.  
`open.open_mid_situation`

### The Stated Promise

**Also called:** the explicit contract, telling them what they'll get
**What it is:** The opening says out loud what the piece will deliver, and the piece then delivers it.
**Effect on the audience:** A reason to stay expressed as a transaction. It is unsubtle and it works.
**Used for and where it works best:** Explainer, instructional, vlog, advertising, educational and most non-fiction short-form. In long-form YouTube the promise belongs in the first thirty seconds and the piece dies from minute two without one. This is one of the few places where being on the nose is correct rather than a failure — see `dial.on_the_nose`, which lists this as a legitimate use.
**Best in:** formats: Explainer, Vlog, Educational, Advertising, Podcast, Documentary | genres: Educational, Science, Advocacy, Journalism, Lifestyle, Heritage
**Avoid when:** Drama of any kind. A promise stated aloud in fiction is a summary, and the audience does not need a story they have already been told. And a promise is a payoff, not an itinerary: *in this video I'll cover three things* is the summarising line `open.nut_graf` finds the retention curve breaking on, and a piece that opens on a scene states its stake after that scene instead.
**Example:**
> *By the end of this you'll know why every one of these buildings has the same crack in the same place.*

**Yields to:** `open.contract_opening` — Drama, where a spoken promise becomes a summary.  
`open.stated_promise`

### The Loop Opening

**Also called:** the seamless restart, the rewatch open
**What it is:** The opening is written so that it follows naturally from the ending, so that a looping playback reads as continuous.
**Effect on the audience:** Involuntary rewatch, which platforms count.
**Used for and where it works best:** Reels, Shorts and TikTok, where the loop is a measured metric. The strongest version makes the second viewing *mean something different* — the opening line that was innocuous now carries the ending's information. That version is craft; a merely seamless join is a trick.
**Best in:** formats: Reels/Shorts, Vertical Micro-Drama, Short Animation, Advertising | genres: Comedy, Thriller, Psychological, Melodrama, Educational
**Avoid when:** The loop is being used to conceal that the piece has no ending. A loop must add meaning, rhythm or replay value, never hide an absence.
**Shelf life:** dated — review 2027-09. Loop weighting in platform ranking is current practice.
**Example:**
> **First line:** "He never found out."
> **Last line:** "Don't tell him."

`open.loop_opening`

## Openings that fail

### The False Start

**Also called:** the dream opening, the fake-out beginning
**What it is:** The opening turns out not to have happened — a dream, a fantasy, a film within the film, a lie later corrected.
**Effect on the audience:** Distrust, usually. Every fake-out spends credit, and the opening is when the audience has least to spend.
**Used for and where it works best:** Rarely, and only when the falseness is itself the subject — a story about self-deception, an unreliable narrator established immediately, a comedy where the deflation is the joke. If used, reveal the falseness fast, within the same scene, so it reads as a statement of method rather than as a trick.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Novel, Half-Hour Comedy, Animation | genres: Comedy, Psychological, Satire, Surreal, Horror
**Avoid when:** Almost always. The dream opening is the single most recognisable amateur signal in unsolicited submissions, precisely because it delivers excitement the writer has not yet earned. If the opening is good, do not retract it; if it is not, do not open with it.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** three pages of a chase, then she wakes up.
> **Working:** three lines of a chase, then — *That is not what happened, but it is what I told the police.*

**Yields to:** `voice.unstable_authority` — The falseness is the subject; unreliable teller, not a retraction.  
`open.false_start`

### The Backstory Open

**Also called:** starting before the beginning, the prologue trap
**What it is:** Opening with the history that led to the story rather than with the story.
**Effect on the audience:** Patience spent on people they have not met yet.
**Used for and where it works best:** Almost never in that raw form, but there are two legitimate versions. **One:** a prologue in a *different* time or register that poses a question the main narrative will answer — this works because it is a hook, not history. **Two:** heritage and historical work where the audience genuinely lacks the context and the context is itself interesting.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Heritage Documentary, Limited Series, Feature Film | genres: Heritage, Historical, Fantasy, Epic, War
**Avoid when:** The standard case. The reliable test: cut the first chapter or the first ten pages and see whether anything is missing. In most drafts nothing is, and what was lost can be redistributed — see `scene.absorb_and_delete`.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** four pages on how the family acquired the land in 1948.
> **Working:** 1948, one page, a man burying something. Then 2026, and the digger arrives.

**Yields to:** `open.prologue_other_register` — The history is needed; offset it in time or register.  
`open.backstory_open`

### The Weather Open

**Also called:** setting before subject, the establishing paragraph
**What it is:** Opening with place, weather or atmosphere before any person, want or event.
**Effect on the audience:** Nothing, which is the problem. Atmosphere is only felt by a reader who has a reason to be somewhere.
**Used for and where it works best:** Two cases only. In literary fiction where the place *is* the subject and the prose is the hook — then this is `open.voice_hook` wearing a coat. And in heritage or nature documentary, where the landscape is the protagonist. In both, the description must do something a character cannot.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Documentary, Heritage Documentary, Essay | genres: Literary, Nature, Heritage, Historical
**Avoid when:** Everywhere else. The diagnostic: if the first person appears after the third paragraph, move them to the first.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** two paragraphs on the heat, then a man walks in.
> **Working:** *The heat had been going on so long that Kareem had stopped calling it the heat and started calling it the situation.*

**Yields to:** `open.voice_hook` — Literary work where the place is the subject and prose is the hook.  
`open.weather_open`

### The Overload Open

**Also called:** too many names, the crowded first page
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** An opening that introduces more people, places or terms than a reader can hold.
**Effect on the audience:** Quiet withdrawal. Readers rarely complain about this; they simply stop, and cannot say why.
**Used for and where it works best:** Nowhere as a technique — listed here as a named failure so it can be diagnosed. The working limit is roughly three named people and one invented term on a first page, and fewer in short-form. Ensemble work does not escape this; it stages the introductions instead.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always. The fix is sequencing, not cutting: the same twelve characters introduced across four scenes cause no difficulty at all.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** six names, two cities and an organisation in one paragraph.
> **Working:** one man, one room, one letter. The other five arrive over the next thirty pages.

**Yields to:** `open.first_paragraph_contents` — The first-page budget that prevents the crowding.  
`open.overload_open`

### The Unearned Stakes Open

**Also called:** caring before knowing, the hollow threat
**What it is:** Opening with something enormous at risk — a death, a city, a war — before the audience has any attachment to what is threatened.
**Effect on the audience:** Indifference dressed as spectacle. Stakes are a function of attachment, not of scale, so a threat to strangers is information rather than tension.
**Used for and where it works best:** Only when the spectacle is itself the promise — disaster, action, and certain science fiction, where the audience has come for scale and will accept it before attachment. Even there, the convention is to give one named person inside the spectacle.
**Best in:** formats: Feature Film, Game Narrative, Animation Feature | genres: Action, Disaster, Science Fiction, War, Horror
**Avoid when:** Drama of every kind, and in any short-form. The repair is almost always to shrink: replace the city with one household, and the threat becomes legible.
**Example:**
> **Failing:** the dam will fail and forty thousand will die.
> **Working:** the dam will fail, and Abu Sattar has already moved his mother's bed upstairs twice this year.

**Yields to:** `open.character_hook` — Shrink to one person the audience can attach to.  
`open.unearned_stakes`

## Openings by position

### The Series Opening

**Also called:** the pilot problem, the first-episode double job
**What it is:** An opening that must do two incompatible things: tell a complete satisfying story now, and promise a hundred more.
**Effect on the audience:** A decision about whether to commit weeks rather than minutes.
**Used for and where it works best:** Pilots and first episodes. The workable solution is to close the episode's question and open the series' question in the same beat — resolve what was asked in minute one, and let the resolution create the standing condition the series will run on. A pilot that only sets up is not a pilot; a pilot that only concludes has no series.
**Best in:** formats: One-Hour Drama, Half-Hour Comedy, Limited Series, Web Series, Vertical Micro-Drama, Podcast | genres: Crime, Drama, Comedy, Procedural, Science Fiction, Family Drama
**Avoid when:** Limited series and anthologies, where the second job does not exist and the first episode can behave like the first act of a film.
**Example:**
> The case closes. In closing it she has to sign her name to something untrue, and the person who asked her to is her new partner.

`open.series_opening`

### The Episode Opening

**Also called:** the re-entry, the returning audience problem
**What it is:** An opening written for an audience who already knows the world, may have forgotten the details, and may be arriving after a gap.
**Effect on the audience:** Either seamless return or the small irritation of being told what they remember.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every episodic form. The working principle is to reorient through *action* rather than recap — someone doing something that only makes sense in light of last week reminds the audience of last week without a recap. In short-form serials the reorientation is compressed to one line, usually an accusation.
**Best in:** formats: One-Hour Drama, Half-Hour Comedy, Web Series, Vertical Micro-Drama, Podcast, Animation Series | genres: Crime, Procedural, Drama, Comedy, Melodrama, Family Drama
**Avoid when:** The first episode, and any binge-designed release where the audience arrives thirty seconds after the last one ended — there, recap is friction.
**Example:**
> She is changing the locks. She does not explain. Anyone who watched last week knows exactly why, and anyone who did not now knows enough.

**Yields to:** `open.series_opening` — The first episode, which carries a second job.  
`open.episode_opening`

### The Chapter Opening

**Also called:** the section start, re-entering prose
**What it is:** How a chapter or section begins after a break, which is a different problem from how a book begins.
**Effect on the audience:** Whether they continue now or put the book down at the break — which is the actual moment readers stop.
**Used for and where it works best:** Novels and long-form non-fiction. Two reliable methods: start the chapter later in time than the reader expects, forcing them to catch up; or open on a line that revises something they believed at the end of the previous chapter. Both work because a chapter break is a small ending, and the next opening must re-hook rather than resume.
**Best in:** formats: Novel, Novella, Memoir, Long-Form Non-Fiction, Serialised Fiction | genres: all prose
**Avoid when:** The chapter continues a scene across the break, where re-hooking is disruptive. There, continue plainly.
**Example:**
> Previous chapter ends: *He said he would call in the morning.*
> Next chapter opens: *He called eleven years later.*

`open.chapter_opening`

### The Scene Opening

**Also called:** the micro-open, entering a scene
**What it is:** The technique of opening any individual scene, as distinct from opening the work.
**Effect on the audience:** Cumulative. A work in which every scene opens on arrival is slow no matter how good its first page was.
**Used for and where it works best:** Everywhere, as a pass of its own. Cut the first three lines of every scene in a draft and read it again — in most cases nothing is lost. See `scene.late_entry` for the full treatment; this card exists so the technique is reachable from an openings search as well as a scene search.
**Best in:** formats: all narrative | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** The arrival is the content — a homecoming, an unwelcome entrance, a first meeting.
**Example:**
> **Before:** He parks, walks up, knocks, she opens, they sit, "So what did the lawyer say?"
> **After:** "So what did the lawyer say?"

**Yields to:** `scene.arrival_scene` — The arrival is the content: a homecoming, an entrance.  
`open.scene_opening`
